Water is also among what Allah has provided you, but it is singled out and mentioned explicitly before the other provisions because that is the first thing that one would request when surrounded by intense heat. The meaning of the verse should be clear.

(7:51) Those who took their religion for diversion (lahwan) and play (laʿiban) and whom the life of the world had deceived (gharrat, from ghurūr). So today We will forget them (nansāhum, from nisyān) as they forgot the encounter of this day of theirs, and as they used to impugn (yajʿadūna, from jaʿd) Our signs.

Lahw is “anything that distracts one from what is more important.” Laʿib means “an act that is done out of fancy and imagination, not for a real purpose.” Ghurūr is “pretending to be helpful but intending to harm.” Nisyān (forgetting, forgetfulness) is the opposite of dhikr (remembrance, mindfulness), but it is sometimes used metaphorically when someone ignores and disregards something deliberately, as though it is forgotten. This is how the term is used in this verse. Jaḥd means “to negate, to deny, to reject.”

This verse explains what is meant by the faithless at the end of the last verse. We can infer three interpretations for kufr (disbelief, faithlessness, denial) from this verse: (1) It means taking one’s religion for diversion and play, and being deceived by the life of this world. (2) It means forgetting the day of encountering God. (3) It means denying the signs [and/

or communications] of God. These are all pertinent interpretations for kufr, in one way or another.

Those who took their religion for diversion and play…: This sentence shows that everyone has a religion, even those who engage in diversion and play, and spend their entire life in that way. As we said in our exposition of the verse, Those who bar [others] from the way of Allah, and seek to make it crooked… (7:45), religion is the path that one treads in this life, and there is no escape from it. God has set out this path according to our pristine nature and divine makeup (fiṭrah), and has called us to it [through His prophets]. This is the real religion of humankind which belongs to them [as the verse says their religion]. This is the path that people should pursue, for it leads them to their true purpose, which is a happy [eternal] life. As long as people follow this path and adhere to it, their religion coincides with the religion that God has prescribed according to their innate

human nature. However, if they divert from this path to other occupations which distract them and only lead to material pleasures—which

are rather imaginary objectives—then they have taken their religion to be diversion and play, and the life of this world has deceived them with its illusive attractions.

… So today We will forget them as they forgot the encounter of this day of theirs, and as they used to impugn Our signs: This sentence is similar to the verse: He [God] will say: “So it is. Our signs came to you, but you forgot them, and thus you will be forgotten today” (20:126). Forgetting God’s signs in this verse [20:126] is equivalent to impugning His signs in the current verse; it is a cause for being forsaken by God on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is: “Today We shall ignore them and not provide what they need to lead a happy life, just as they ignored this day of theirs and did not prepare for it by doing what was incumbent upon them, and because they used to reject Our signs [and/or communications].”

(7:52) Certainly We have brought them a Book, which We have elaborated with knowledge, as a guidance and mercy for a people who have

faith.

This verse ties back to the beginning of this set of verses: So who is a greater wrongdoer than him who fabricates a lie against Allah, or denies His signs? (7:37). The meaning is: “So who is a greater wrongdoer than these people given that We have completed Our proof against them and have clarified Our message [of guidance] for them? We have done so by bringing them a Book which We have elaborated for them. We have revealed

this Book to them while We have complete knowledge about its revelation.” With knowledge qualifies the verb “bring” in We have brought them a Book. This effectively implies an argument for the truth of the Book: “We have brought them a scripture which consists of the truth because its revelation has been according to Our knowledge [which is a hundred percent accurate]. We are fully aware of the content of this Book.”1

This is a good answer by the author of al-Manār, but we should clarify that we do not consider a solitary report (khabar al-wāḥid) to be authoritative (ḥujjah) unless it is coupled with decisive evidence which result in

definite knowledge for the individual [scholar]. This is applicable to all solitary reports, whether about historical accounts, merits of individuals, or other topics. The only exception is jurisprudence, where collective

acceptance of a narration [by a number of scholars] is sufficient for its authority. Of course, all of this is conditional on the narration not contravening the Qur’an. Further details should be pursued in principles of

jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh).

Making this announcement is certainly a merit for the Imam, and this is nothing to be disputed. We can infer the significance of announcement in the hereafter by reflecting on its significance in this world.

Announcement means making a declaration on behalf of a ruler to those who are subject to that rule. A muʾadhdhin (caller, announcer) is a link which connects the ruler to the ruled by stating the ruler’s judgment to the subjects. The merit or demerit of a link is according to what it connects to. Being a connecting link to God would certainly be an unsurpassed merit and excellence for that link. An example of this can be seen in the intermediation of Abraham in making God’s announcement: And proclaim the hajj to people (22:27). Another example is the intermediation of

Imam ʿAlī in conveying the verses of barāʾah: [This is] an announcement from Allah and His Messenger (9:3).

This is the meaning of announcement in this world, which is a legislative declaration of a rule to those who are subject to it. However,

announcement in the hereafter is not a legislative declaration, but it means causing an event and establishing the reality of a command. In this case [verse 7:44], it means establishing the eternal damnation of wrongdoers and their absolute distance from divine mercy, following their acknowledgment to the truth of God’s promises, which they received through His

prophets and messengers [as mentioned at the beginning of the verse]. This means that the caller on that day will materialize God’s promises and threats to the wrongdoers; he is the one who metes out the consequence of their deeds to them. The reader should reflect on this and should not underestimate the significance of real matters [as opposed to conventional and legislative matters]. This is worthy of further and more rigorous investigation by those who have the aptitude for it.1

The above is what the Imam meant when he referred to himself as being “the caller in this world and the hereafter.” As we saw above, this is narrated in the Shia sources through various chains of narration from Imams ʿAlī, al-Bāqir and al-Riḍā [hadiths 22-24]. It is also narrated in the Sunni sources by al-Ḥākim, from Imam ʿAlī and Ibn ʿAbbās [hadiths 25-26]. Al-Ḥākim is a reliable reporter and transmitter of hadith. He is often quoted in commentaries that are based on hadith as well as other commentaries in general. However, none of the Sunni exegetes has quoted him on this narration; even someone like al-Suyūṭī—who has an exhaustive coverage of narrations in al-Durr al-manthūr—has lefiiout this hadith.
